was imposed upon M/s Privasia Holdings Pvt. Ltd. (importer company and supplier) 
whereas penalty of Rs. 15,000/ each was imposed upon Shri Vimal Kishore, Appellant no. 1 (FBO cumManager) and M/s Jubilant Food Works Ltd, FBO Unit, Appellant no. 2  herein, for selling the food article 'Sweet Corn' without declaration of "Best before date"

3. Feeling aggrieved, the appellants have challenged the impugned order mainly on  the following grounds;

4. The facts giving rise to this appeal are that on 31.01.2012 at about 7 pm, Food & 
Safety Officer, Sh. Suniti Kumar Gupta lifted a sample of 'Sweet Corn' from Sh. Vimal  Kishore S/o Dr. Suresh Kumar, Domino Pizza (a Unit of M/s Jubilant Food Works Ltd), 
Saket PVR New Delhi17 for analysis under the Food Safety and Standard Act 2006 and  Rules/Regulations made there under (hereinafter referred to as FSS Act).
Efforts  were made to get the public witness to join the sample proceedings but none came forward and  on request, Ms. Usha Kiran, FSO joined as witness to the sample  proceedings.

The sample consisted of eight sealed tins each containing 8 x 285 grams  of 'Sweet Corn' taken as such in original condition bearing identical label declaration. 
The sample was divided into four equal parts then and there by the FSO by converting  one sealed tin of 'Sweet Corn' as one counter part of the sample.

Each counterpart  containing the sample was separately packed, fastened, sealed and the signatures of  FBO were obtained on the D.O. slip and wrapper of the tins containing the sample as per  the prescribed procedure.
The panchnama in Form V A was prepared and the  signature of Sh. Vimal Kishore (appellant no. 1), FBO was obtained as a token of its  acknowledgment.
A price of Rs. 400/ was paid to the appellant no. 1 vide Food  Business Operator receipt dated 31.01.2012.

Thereafter, one counter part of the  aforesaid sample bearing Designated Officer's code number 08/DO04/1343 alongwith  one copy of form VI in a sealed packet and another copy of memo in Form VI in a separate sealed  cover were sent separately to Food Analyst, Delhi for analysis on  01.02.2012.
The FBO did not request to send the fourth part of the sample for analysis  from NABL, Accredited Laboratory under Rule 2.4.5 of the Food Safety and Standards  Rules, 2011.

Another two counterparts of the sample in a sealed packet alongwith two  copies of form VI as well as the fourth counterpart in a separate sealed packet alongwith one copy  of form VI were deposited with Designated Officer Sh. 2 01.02.2012.
The Food Analyst vide his report no. PFA/Enf./229/2012 dated 10.02.2012

has reported that "the sample is misbranded because there is violation of Regulation  No. 2.2.2.10 of the Food Safety and Standards (Packaging and Labeling) Regulation, 
2011.

Consequently, a complaint was filed  against six persons including the appellants herein before the Ld. ADM South, who after  hearing all the parties enforced a penalty of Rs. 15,000/ each upon appellant no. 1 and  2 and Rs. 20,000/ on the respondent no. 6 M/s Privasia Holdings Pvt. Ltd. (therein) for  violation of regulation no. 2.2.2.10 of the FSS Act (packages and labelling regulation). 
5.
I have heard the rival contentions advanced on behalf of both the parties and have  carefully perused the trial court record.

6. The main contention raised by the Ld. Counsel for the appellants is that the  appellants had purchased the articles sweet corn from M/s. Privasia Holdings Pvt. Ltd. in  a sealed condition and sold further in the same condition against the proper bills/invoice  bearing serial no. 2044 dated 21.11.2011 issued by M/s Privasia Holdings Pvt. Ltd. and  the said supply to the appellant no. 2 was not disputed by M/s Privasia Holdings Pvt. Ltd. during  the adjudication proceedings.
Even the packets of the sweet corn were not  tampered with in any manner.
As per the Public Analyst Report, the sampled article was  conformed to standard but the same was opined to be misbranded on account non  mentioning of "Best Before date".

He further argued that the appellants were neither the  manufacturer nor the packer of the sampled commodity and thus, the defence of due  diligence should have been extended to them and as such, the appellants were liable to
be protected by the warranty of M/s Privasia Holdings Pvt. Ltd. as provided in Section
80 (B)(2)(d)(i) of the FSS Act, 2006 read with Section 26(4) of the FSS Act who was

the  importer/supplier of the sampled article and appellant's role was limited to sale of the  sealed packet in the same condition as purchased by them from M/s Privasia Holdings  Pvt. Ltd. and as such, impugned order is not sustainable against them.

To support his contentions, 
he has placed reliance upon the judgment P. Unnikrishnan Vs. Food  Inspector, Palghat Municipally, Palghat, Kerala State, AIR 1995 SC 1983 wherein  t h e i r l o r d s h i p s w e r e p l e a s e d t o h e l d t h a t   C r i m i n a l - C o n v i c t i o n - S e c t i o n 1 9 ( 2 ) o f P r e v e n t i o n o f F o o d  Adulteration Act - Magistrate had acquitted Accused who were tried for an offence under  Section 7(1) read with Section 16(1A)(a)(i) of Act - High Court had reversed order  o f a c q u i t t a l a n d c o n v i c t e d A p p e l l a n t - H e n c e , t h i s A p p e a l -

7. Per contra, the Ld. Addl. PP has refuted the entire line of arguments whilst making  submissions that the Food Safety Officer was within its power to lift the sample of Sweet  Corn.
The copy of the notice as per Form VA was given to FBO and panchnama was prepared on  the spot.
All the documents prepared by FSO were read over and  explained to Sh. Vimal Kishore who signed the same after having admitted their contents  to be correct.
Not only this, he did not make any request to the FSO regarding sending  one sample part to Accredited Lab for testing.

It cannot be ignored that the same was  kept for human consumption and the same is opined to be misbranded because of  violation of Regulation No. 2.2.2.10 of the FSS Act (packages and labelling regulation) 
and as such, it comes within the mischief of section 26(2)(ii) of the FSS Act r/w section  3(1)(zf)(C) (i) of FSS Act which is punishable under Section 52 of the FSS Act. 
8.
Before proceeding further, let me quote the relevant statutory provision: Section 2  (ix) of the Prevention of Food Adulteration Act, 1954 describes 'misbranding' of an article  of food.

The relevant clause 'k' relating to label reads as under :
" 2 ( i x ) m i s b r a n d e d  a n a r t i c l e o f f o o d s h a l l b e d e e m e d t o b e  misbranded - (a) to (j).....
( k ) I f i t i s n o t l a b e l e d i n a c c o r d a n c e w i t h t h e r e q u i r e m e n t s o f  this Act or Rules made thereunder".

F u r t h e r m o r e , ' M i s b r a n d e d ' a s d e f i n e d i n S e c t i o n 2 ( i x ) o f t h e  Act and interpreted by the Hon'ble Supreme Court reported in the case of "Bal Kishan Thakur  Vs. Municipal Corporation, Delhi" reported in AIR 1979 SC 1004. 
9.

sentences.text: In the present case the allegation against the appellants were that the sampled  product was without declaration of best before date and is thus, misbranded.
But no  reason has been given by the Analyst for declaring the sample to be misbranded and  infact, the sample was conformed to standard.
The objective of the declaration of the  label
was that the purchaser should know at the time of purchase as to whether the  article purchased was capable of being used and till what time.

But the appellants in the  instant case cannot be held responsible for not mentioning the best before date as the  sample lifted was purchased from M/s Privasia Holdings Pvt. Ltd. in a sealed condition  vide bill bearing Sl no. 2044.

However the sample conform to standard"
11.

The relevant statutory provision which is pivot of the case in question is produced below:
 Sec 80. Defences which may or may not be allowed in  prosecution under this Act.

(A) .....
 (B) Defence of due diligence-- (1).....
 (2) Without limiting the ways in which a person may satisfy the requirements  of clause (1), a person satisfies those requirements if it is proved - Sh. Vimal Kishore vs State on 15 March, 2017 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/76262855/
5  (a).....
 (b)....
 (c)....
 (d) in the case of an offence involving the sale of food, that--  ( i ) T h e p e r s o n s o l d t h e f o o d i n t h e s a m e c o n d i t i o n  as and when the person purchased it. 
12.

From the material available on record, it stands established that the appellants  were the retailer/seller and not manufacturer of the sampled article and the sampled  article was purchased by the appellants from M/s Privasia Holdings Pvt. Ltd. in the  sealed condition and as such, the appellants cannot be prosecuted for a product which  is alleged to be misbranded.
The appellants sold it in the same manner and condition in which it  was purchased by them.
The manufacturer from whom the appellants  purchased the article has been duly licensed, depends on the facts of the case.
In every  case, the accused cannot be expected to verify further whether the contents of the label  on the tin and those in the bill containing the warranty are correct or not.

In the instant  case, the sampled article i.e. sweet corn was imported by M/s Privasia Holdings Pvt. 
Ltd. and was supplied/sold to the appellants in a sealed condition and also issued an  invoice bearing Sl. No. 2044 dated 21.11.2011 having the warranty.

At that juncture, no  knowledge about the nonexistence of the firm could be attributed to the appellants and  they could not be expected to verify as to what the actual position was regarding the  existence of the firm at place who is an importer.

It may be that the firm was in existence  and if for any reason subsequently the firm does not exist, then appellants cannot be deprived of  the defence to which he is entitled to under section 19(2).

Since the  allegation in the complaint is with regard to non mentioning of best before date on the  tins and not about the product itself, it is clear that the appellants have not committed any offence  and therefore, I find force in the contention of the Ld. Counsel for the appellants.

13. On the basis of reappreciation of the material from the trial court record, I am of  the considered view that the court of Ld. Adjudicating Officer fell into an error and failed  to appreciate the statutory provision which is pivot of the case and in this regard, the  order of the Ld. Adjudicating Officer is vitiated with error of law, impropriety and mis appreciation  of the material qua the appellants and in this context, I feel every justification to  i n t e r f e r e i n t h e i m p u g n e d o r d e r p a s s e d b y t h e L d . 
Adjudicating Officer.
Thus, the impugned order dated 15/16.09.2015 is set aside qua the  claim of the appellants by accepting the appeal.
Copy of this judgment be placed in the  trial court record and thereafter, TCR be sent back to the concerned court.
Appeal file be  consigned to the record room.
